ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Prion diseases are fatal, slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorders caused by misfolded prion protein that spreads in the brain. They present with rapidly worsening dementia, myoclonus, and ataxia, and are invariably fatal.

sections.p: Prion diseases are caused by an abnormal isoform of the normal cellular prion protein (PrP^C). The misfolded form (PrP^Sc) aggregates, induces other PrP^C to misfold, and spreads through neural tissue, producing spongiform changes and neuronal loss.
Prions are not alive; they are proteinaceous infectious particles lacking nucleic acid. They are resistant to standard sterilisation and can be transmitted via contaminated tissue.
b: Highly resistant to heat, radiation, chemicals

sections.p: Human prion diseases arise sporadically, genetically, or through iatrogenic exposure. Transmission occurs via contaminated surgical instruments, transplanted tissues, or consumption of infected meat.

t.b: Confirms spongiform change and PrP^Sc deposition; definitive diagnosis when available
Positive in most CJD cases; indicates rapid neuronal death
Periodic sharp wave complexes suggest CJD; non‑specific
Hyperintensity in basal ganglia/cortex supports CJD diagnosis

sections.p: The most common human form is sporadic Creutzfeldt‑Jakob disease (sCJD). Other forms include familial CJD, Gerstmann‑Straussler‑Scheinker syndrome, fatal familial insomnia, and kuru.
b: Rapid progression over weeks to months

sections.p: Diagnosis relies on clinical features, imaging, CSF biomarkers, and, when possible, brain biopsy. The WHO criteria combine major and minor findings.

t.b: Detects cortical ribboning; highly sensitive for sCJD
Positive in ~90% of sCJD; supportive but not specific
Characteristic but seen in other encephalopathies

sections.p: No disease‑modifying therapy exists. Management is supportive: antiepileptics for seizures, benzodiazepines for myoclonus, and palliative care. Infection control uses high‑level disinfection and instrument segregation.
b: Avoid routine autopsies of brain tissue

sections.p: Remember that prion diseases are invariably fatal and that diagnosis is largely clinical with supportive investigations. Iatrogenic transmission is a key public‑health issue.
b: Prion diseases are not infectious by droplets or airborne routes

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, or ataxia; any unexplained neurological decline in a patient with a history of neurosurgery or exposure to animal products

faq.a: Avoid iatrogenic exposure by using dedicated instruments and proper sterilisation; limit consumption of high‑risk animal products in endemic areas.

faq.q: Do prion diseases spread between people?
faq.a: Only via contaminated surgical instruments, transplanted tissues, or rarely through blood transfusion; not by casual contact.

faq.q: Is there a cure for CJD?
faq.a: No; treatment is supportive and palliative.
